deep.reconstruction:
The page has no derivations, numbers or equations. It holds a single careful ink construction with letter labels. The interpretive parts below are my own reading of the image.

What is drawn:
(i) A long, slightly inclined base line runs across the bottom of the page.
(ii) At its right end, at a point marked with a small label (probably p), a vertical line rises to the top right corner.
(iii) A long transversal runs from the top of the vertical line down to the left, meeting the base line. Near its foot it is labelled 'a+p+d-180'.
(iv) Successively shorter transversals join points on the vertical line to points on the base line. They form a family of nearly parallel lines whose feet crowd toward the corner p, a 'fan' or zig-zag converging on the vertex.
(v) Two parallel lines are drawn perpendicular to the transversals, slanting down to the right toward the corner p. The upper one starts at point b on the big transversal. The lower one starts at point a on the same transversal.

Labels at the crossings:
- Upper perpendicular: b, d, b', d, b'', d.
- Lower perpendicular: a, c (written twice), a, c', a, c''.
- So the figure repeats a basic cell with corners a, b, c, d: a strip between two transversals, cut by the two perpendiculars. Each new cell repeats the pattern one step closer to p, with primes marking the iteration.
- Small angle labels: near the first a, probably 'b+v' (written rotated); at the second a, 'b+v' again; along the second transversal near the vertical line, 'p-v'.

My interpretation (uncertain):
- The letters a, b, c, d, p, v appear to denote angles.
- 'a+p+d-180' is the deviation of an angle sum from 180 degrees. This could be an angular excess or defect, or the angle between the first transversal and the base line, obtained by the exterior-angle theorem from angles a, p, d.
- The repeated cells would then show that each successive transversal turns by the same increment, so the configuration repeats self-similarly toward the vertex.
- This is the typical picture of a ray reflected back and forth between two plane mirrors (or lines) meeting at p, each step rotating the direction by a fixed angle. It could also be a geometric illustration of an instrument (reflecting or repeating instrument) or of error propagation.
- The neighbouring pages are astronomical: page 296 has only the numbers 3500/4500/5500; page 298 has Polaris culminations with a least-squares mean error. So an instrumental or optical purpose is plausible, but this cannot be confirmed from the page alone.

Nothing on the page is a written derivation. The content is the elementary angle-chasing implied by the figure: angle sums in triangles, the exterior-angle theorem, and parallel or perpendicular transfer of angles.
errors: No computational steps are present, so none can be checked for error.
The figure is drawn freehand-accurately but is not to exact scale: the transversals are only nearly parallel. Any metric reading of the diagram is therefore unreliable.

checkable.asserts: Hypothetical reading: in a triangle with two interior angles 180-a and 180-p-d, the third angle equals a+p+d-180 (angle sum 180). This is consistent with the label on the long transversal.
